unit-phys-ramp.title: Kinematics 1 · The Ramp Lab
unit-phys-ramp.source: Physics 8, Kinematics — 'Ramp Lab' procedure and questions (Drive)

summary.text: The Ramp Lab measures a ball's average acceleration rolling down a ramp, from position and time data. The twist is graphical: a position-vs-time graph for accelerated motion is a curve, not a straight line, so before you can pull a slope out of it, you have to LINEARIZE it — usually by plotting position against time-squared instead, which turns the curve into a straight line whose slope reveals the acceleration.

why.text: Linearizing shows up constantly once labs stop being simple constant-velocity motion — any time the raw data is curved, finding the right thing to plot on the x-axis to straighten it out is the actual analysis skill, more than the ball, the ramp, or the stopwatch.

objectives.text: Explain why a position-vs-time graph for accelerated motion is curved, not straight.
Explain what linearizing the graph accomplishes and why plotting against t² works.
Predict how ramp steepness and location (Earth vs. Moon) change measured acceleration.
Explain why giving the ball a push changes v₀ but not the acceleration itself.
Solve average-speed problems, including recognizing when the target average is impossible.

parentNote.text: Built from the Ramp Lab handout's procedure and its five conceptual/short-answer questions. The lab itself asks her to collect real data (distance, time, velocity, acceleration) and analyze it graphically — that data doesn't exist yet, so this unit covers the REASONING behind the lab (why linearize, what changes the result) rather than inventing numbers for a data set that's hers to collect. The one numeric question on the sheet (the average-speed word problem) is echoed here with fresh numbers, verified independently with sympy, plus a second version that lands on a real, achievable answer rather than an impossible one — the lab's own version turns out to be impossible as written, which is worth knowing before she's staring at it expecting a normal number.

nextUp.text: Read the cards once before lab day — the linearizing idea is the one thing worth having straight before you're staring at a curved graph in class.

cards.term: Why a position–time graph curves under acceleration
cards.def:
**Because position depends on t², not just t — so equal time steps cover growing distances.**
• Δx = v₀t + ½at² has a t² term, which is what makes the graph bend upward.
• A straight line only happens when acceleration is zero (constant velocity).
cards.hint: t² in the formula = a curve on the graph.

cards.def:
**Plotting position against TIME-SQUARED (t²) instead of time turns the curve into a straight line.**
• Since Δx = v₀t + ½at², plotting Δx vs. t² makes the t² term the x-axis itself — the relationship becomes linear.
• A straight line's slope is easy to measure and trust; a curve's "slope" keeps changing, so you can't just draw one line through it.
cards.hint: Curve in x-vs-t → straight line in x-vs-t².
cards.eq: slope of Δx vs. t² = ½a

cards.term: Getting acceleration from the linearized slope
cards.def:
**The slope of the linearized (Δx vs. t²) graph equals ½a, so a = 2 × slope.**
• This is the whole point of linearizing — once it's straight, ordinary slope math (rise over run) gets you the acceleration directly.
• Forgetting to double the slope is the single most common mistake with this graph.
cards.hint: Slope is HALF of a — always double it.

cards.def:
**A steeper ramp always produces a LARGER acceleration.**
• Only part of gravity's pull acts along a tilted ramp's surface; a steeper angle redirects more of it along the ramp instead of into it.
• At a full 90° (straight down), the ball would accelerate at the full value of g.
cards.hint: Steeper ramp = more of gravity pointing down the slope.

cards.def:
**Giving the ball a push changes its INITIAL velocity (v₀) — not its acceleration.**
• Acceleration on a ramp comes from the ramp's angle (and gravity), which a push doesn't touch.
• A pushed ball starts faster and covers the ramp quicker, but it speeds up at exactly the same RATE as an un-pushed one.
cards.hint: A push changes the starting speed, not the rate of speeding up.

cards.def:
**On the Moon, where gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's, the same ramp would produce about 1/6 the acceleration.**
• Ramp acceleration is always some fraction of local gravity — shrink gravity, and the ramp's acceleration shrinks by the same fraction.
• The ball would take noticeably longer to roll the same distance, and the linearized graph's slope would come out about 1/6 as steep.
cards.hint: Ramp acceleration scales directly with whatever gravity you're standing under.

cards.term: Average speed isn't the average of the speeds
cards.def:
**"Average speed over a whole trip" means total distance ÷ total time — NOT the arithmetic average of the speeds on each leg.**
• A slow leg costs disproportionate TIME, not just "one slow number to average in."
• Always work in total distance and total time, never by averaging the speed values directly.
cards.hint: Add up distances and times separately — then divide.

cards.term: When a target average speed is impossible
cards.def:
**If the time already spent on earlier legs meets or exceeds the whole trip's allowed time, no finishing speed — however fast — can fix the average.**
• Check the running time total against the trip's time budget before solving for what's left.
• This is the trap in a surprising number of "what speed do I need" problems — the answer is sometimes "there isn't one."
cards.hint: Compare time spent so far to total time allowed — first, before solving anything.

questions.q: A student collects position and time data for a ball speeding up on a ramp, then plots position (y-axis) against time (x-axis). What shape should the raw data form?
opts: A straight line through the origin
A straight line with a negative slope
questions.hint: Does position depend on t, or on t²?
steps: Position under constant acceleration follows Δx = v₀t + ½at².
The t² term means position grows faster and faster as time goes on.
That growing rate of change is exactly what a curve, bending upward, looks like on a graph.

ex.main: **A curve, bending upward.** The t² term is what bends the line — a straight line only happens when acceleration is zero.
ex.tip: If a graph should be curved but comes out straight (or vice versa), that's a sign to double-check for constant acceleration.

questions.q: Why can't you just draw a line of best fit through the raw position-vs-time data from an accelerating ball?
opts: Because the data is curved, and a straight line can't accurately fit a curve
Because position-vs-time graphs are never useful
Because a ruler cannot be used on a computer graph
Because you need at least 20 data points to draw any line
questions.hint: What shape is the raw data, and what shape is a "line of best fit"?
steps: A line of best fit is, by definition, straight.
The raw position-vs-time data from accelerated motion is curved, not straight.
Forcing a straight line through curved data would badly misrepresent it — the data needs to be linearized first.

ex.main: **Because the data is curved.** A straight line drawn through curved data doesn't actually describe the data — it has to be linearized first.
ex.tip: "Should I draw a line of best fit?" always starts with "is this data actually straight?"

questions.q: To linearize position-vs-time data from an accelerating object, what should be plotted on the x-axis instead of plain time?
questions.hint: Which term in Δx = v₀t + ½at² is the one causing the curve?
steps: The curve comes from the t² term in Δx = v₀t + ½at².
Plotting Δx against t² (instead of t) turns that t² term into a plain linear relationship.
The result is a straight line whose slope is ½a.

ex.main: **Time squared (t²).** Once t² is the x-axis, the relationship between it and position is a straight line.
ex.tip: Whatever term is bending the graph is usually the thing to put on the new x-axis.

questions.q: A linearized graph (position vs. t²) has a measured slope of 1.5 m/s². What is the ball's acceleration?
questions.hint: The slope of this particular graph equals HALF the acceleration.
steps: The slope of a Δx-vs-t² graph equals ½a, not a itself.
So a = 2 × slope.

ex.main: **3 m/s².** Doubling the slope is the one step that's easy to forget on this particular graph.
ex.tip: Always ask "is this graph's slope equal to a, or to ½a, or to something else?" before reading a value off it.

questions.q: Two identical ramps are set at different angles: Ramp A at 20° and Ramp B at 40°. A ball is released from rest on each. Which statement is correct?
opts: Ramp B produces a larger acceleration than Ramp A
Both ramps produce exactly the same acceleration
Ramp A produces a larger acceleration than Ramp B
Acceleration depends only on the ball's mass, not the ramp's angle
questions.hint: Which ramp redirects more of gravity's pull along its own surface?
steps: A steeper ramp redirects more of gravity's downward pull along the ramp's own direction.
40° is steeper than 20°.
So Ramp B, the steeper one, produces the larger acceleration.

ex.main: **Ramp B produces a larger acceleration.** The steeper the ramp, the more of gravity acts along the direction of motion instead of into the ramp's surface.
ex.tip: Mass doesn't affect a ramp's acceleration at all — a heavier and lighter ball released from rest speed up at the same rate.

questions.q: A student runs the exact same ramp lab on the Moon, where gravity is about 1/6 of Earth's. Compared to the Earth version, what happens to the measured acceleration?
opts: It becomes zero, since there's no air on the Moon
questions.hint: Ramp acceleration is always some fraction of local gravity.
steps: A ramp's acceleration is a fraction of whatever gravity is acting — the same ramp angle always redirects the same FRACTION of gravity.
If gravity itself shrinks to 1/6 of Earth's value, the ramp's acceleration shrinks by that same 1/6 fraction.
So the Moon version's acceleration comes out to about 1/6 of the Earth version's.

ex.main: **About 1/6 as large.** Whatever fraction of gravity a ramp's angle redirects, it does that to whatever gravity IS — shrink gravity, and the result shrinks with it.
ex.tip: Air resistance is a red herring here — the effect on acceleration comes entirely from the change in gravity, not from the presence or absence of air.

questions.q: A ball rolls down a ramp from rest and is measured to accelerate at 2 m/s². A second, identical trial gives the ball a firm push to start it moving at 1.5 m/s down the same ramp. What is the ball's acceleration in the second trial?
opts: Faster than 2 m/s², because it started with extra speed
Slower than 2 m/s², because the push used up some of gravity's pull
0 m/s², because it was already moving
questions.hint: Does a push change the RAMP, or just the ball's starting speed?
steps: Acceleration on a ramp comes from the ramp's angle and gravity — neither of which a push touches.
A push only changes v₀, the ball's starting velocity.
The rate at which the ball speeds up (its acceleration) stays exactly the same: 2 m/s².

ex.main: **Still 2 m/s².** A push changes how fast the ball starts, not how fast it speeds up — those are two separate quantities.
ex.tip: This is a classic mix-up: a bigger starting speed does NOT mean a bigger acceleration.

questions.q: A hiker walks 24 km at a target average speed of 8 km/h. For the first 8 km she manages 12 km/h, and for the next 8 km she only manages 6 km/h. What speed does she need for the final 8 km to still hit her 8 km/h target average?
questions.hint: Add up the time used on the first two legs and compare it to the total time allowed.
steps: Total time allowed: 24 km ÷ 8 km/h = 3 h.
First leg: 8 km ÷ 12 km/h = 2/3 h. Second leg: 8 km ÷ 6 km/h = 4/3 h. Together: 2/3 + 4/3 = 2 h used.
Time left for the final leg: 3 − 2 = 1 h. Required speed: 8 km ÷ 1 h = 8 km/h.

ex.main: **8 km/h.** The faster first leg banked exactly enough extra time to offset the slower second leg — she needs precisely her original target speed for the last stretch.
ex.tip: It's not a coincidence that this comes out equal to the target — check what happens when a fast leg and a slow leg balance out.

questions.q: A cyclist rides 36 km at a target average speed of 18 km/h. For the first 12 km he manages 18 km/h exactly, and for the next 12 km he drops to 9 km/h. What speed does he need for the final 12 km to still hit 18 km/h overall?
opts: About 27 km/h for the last leg
About 36 km/h for the last leg
About 18 km/h for the last leg
questions.hint: Check the time spent on the first two legs against the total time allowed before solving for a speed.
steps: Total time allowed: 36 km ÷ 18 km/h = 2 h.
First leg: 12 km ÷ 18 km/h = 2/3 h. Second leg: 12 km ÷ 9 km/h = 4/3 h. Together: 2/3 + 4/3 = 2 h used.
That's already the ENTIRE 2-hour budget, with 12 km still to go — no finishing speed can make up for zero remaining time.

ex.main: **It's impossible.** The first two legs used up the whole time budget exactly, leaving nothing for the final leg no matter how fast he rides it.
ex.tip: Compare this to the hiker question — same shape of problem, but the numbers here leave no slack at all.

questions.q: A lab group's accepted value for their ramp's acceleration (from the linearized graph) is 2.0 m/s², but a nearby class's textbook lists the expected value as 2.4 m/s². What is the percent error?
steps: Percent error = |measured − accepted| / accepted × 100.

ex.main: **≈16.7%.** Always divide by the ACCEPTED value, not the measured one — the two give different answers.
ex.tip: Dividing by the measured value instead (0.4/2.0 = 20%) is the most common percent-error mistake — check which number is in the denominator.
